answer.evidence: The roof is a large sloped plane that starts as a peak at row 7 and widens row by row to full width at row 19, with shingle courses on both slopes down to a light eave edge line at about rows 45-50. A dark eave shadow line follows it, and the front wall (sign band, brick wall, door, window) runs below to row 111. The two roof planes are shaded differently, but this is not an isometric side wall of the body. The south face is a normal elevation. The roof counts as a sloped top surface (evidence c) above a front face of well over 3 rows.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a whole building like the references, and its visible tones per tile (9) are close to the references (12 and 10). Its dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, so the outlines are tinted (dark grey-blue beside the slate roof, dark tone beside the wall) rather than a black sticker line. Near-flat coverage is 15% against 0% for both references. The roof has about 4 grey steps with some tile-row texture, but it reads as fairly regular and flat. The white stone wall has only light grey block lines and little per-stone shading or speckle, and the blue sign band is a large flat fill with only the text on it. The references have 5-6 steps per material, scalloped tiles with per-tile highlights, plaster speckle and stones shaded one by one. The candidate is cleaner and simpler, and it looks flatter and thinner next to them. Because of the flat fills on the sign band and walls and the shallower ramps, it does not match the Beodeul standard.

The candidate is clearly flatter and simpler than both references, which have rich grain, per-tile shading and speckled plaster or stone. The door and window are decent but small.

The roof is a real sloped plane, not a flat front-facing strip, so the object reads as three-quarter.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate has 9 visible tones per tile against 12 and 10 for the references, so it is near the stone reference but below the timber-and-tile house. Its near-flat coverage is 15% against 0% for both references. That shows in the large uniform areas: the navy sign band, the pale grey wall blocks and the roof planes. The roof does have some slate texture and a few highlight rows, but it is only about 3-4 grey steps with a regular pattern. The references have 5-6 steps with per-tile scallops, plaster speckle and stones shaded one by one. The wall brick lines are thin and regular, with little per-stone variation. The outline is not neutral black (0% near-neutral dark edge pixels) and leans cool and tinted, but it is applied fairly uniformly around the shapes. This reads as a clean, slightly sticker-like building, thinner and flatter than the Beodeul references. When in doubt, fail.

answer.evidence: The roof is a large sloped tile plane (rows 7-49) with a diagonal light fascia/edge line at about rows 45-49 and a dark shadow line at row 50 in the column scan. The roof is shaded light on the left and dark on the right. Below it is a tall south facade (rows ~56-111): a sign, a door, a window and a brick wall. The roof is a sloped plane above an eave line (evidence c), so the building reads as three-quarter, not front elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: The measured facts are close to the references: 9 visible tones per tile against 12 and 10, 0% neutral dark edges, and tinted outlines (grey-blue next to the roof, dark brown on the door). Even so, by eye the candidate is shallower than the Beodeul pieces. The grey roof has only about 4 steps and reads as large flat facets with thin tile lines. It has none of the scalloped tiles with per-tile highlights or the speckle that the references show. The white wall is mostly a flat light grey with simple brick lines and little stone-by-stone shading. The blue sign band is a large flat fill, and the 15% near-flat coverage against 0% for both references confirms this. The result looks cleaner and more sticker-like than the references, so it does not match their richness.
